title: Differentiability of the shape function in the planar corner growth model
notes: Section 6 first proves the bounded-weight case. The full theorem under the stated moment assumptions uses Appendix B.
Lemma B.2 supplies the general-weight proof of Lemma 3.2. Remark 5.8 changes the endpoints and intervals in the general-weight version of Lemma 5.7.

source.title: Differentiability of the shape function in the planar corner growth model

results.label: Theorem 2.1
results.title: The shape is differentiable
results.summary: For independent, identically distributed, nonconstant weights, $g$ is differentiable throughout $\mathbb R_{>0}^2$ if the negative part has a finite moment of some order greater than one and the positive part has a finite moment of some order greater than four. Atoms and signed weights are allowed.

coverage.scope: The full differentiability theorem is certified. The certificate also includes existence and uniqueness of the directional shape, together with the regularity and uniform convergence proved earlier in the paper.

results.label: Theorem 2.2
results.title: Where the shape equals the largest weight
results.summary: For weights with finite largest possible value $M$, the theorem describes the directions where $g(\xi)=M$ and proves differentiability at the ends of that set. Its further classification distinguishes whether the probability of a weight equal to $M$ is below, at, or above the oriented percolation threshold.
definitions: Here $M$ is the smallest real number with $\mathbb P\{\omega_0\le M\}=1$, $p=\mu(\{M\})$, and $g_{\rm top}$ is the directional shape for weights $\mathbf1\{\omega_z=M\}$. A direction is $\xi=(t,1-t)$ with $0\le t\le1$.

In the top-site model a site is open when $\omega_z=M$. The critical probability $p_c$ is the infimum of the independent open-site probabilities for which an infinite up-right open path from the origin has positive probability.

coverage.scope: The certificates describe the top-site flat interval through expected open-path edge rates, prove $g_{\rm top}(\xi)=1\Rightarrow g(\xi)=M$, and prove differentiability at every interior direction of $\mathcal U$ with $g_{\rm top}(\xi)=1$. The normalized edge-rate theorem assumes $0<p<1$. These certificates do not give the classification using $p_c$. They also do not supply the reverse implication $g(\xi)=M\Rightarrow g_{\rm top}(\xi)=1$, or equivalently the strict inequality $g(\xi)<M$ outside the top-site flat set.

restriction.label: Selected flat-segment conclusions
restriction.paper_scope: For a finite upper endpoint $M$, the paper identifies $\{\xi\in\mathcal U:g(\xi)=M\}$ with $\{\xi\in\mathcal U:g_{\rm top}(\xi)=1\}$, classifies this set according to $p<p_c$, $p=p_c$ and $p>p_c$, and proves differentiability at its endpoints.
restriction.certified_scope: The certificates describe the top-site flat interval through expected open-path edge rates, prove $g_{\rm top}(\xi)=1\Rightarrow g(\xi)=M$, and prove differentiability at every interior direction of $\mathcal U$ with $g_{\rm top}(\xi)=1$. The normalized edge-rate theorem assumes $0<p<1$.
restriction.gap: These certificates do not give the classification using $p_c$. They also do not supply the reverse implication $g(\xi)=M\Rightarrow g_{\rm top}(\xi)=1$, or equivalently the strict inequality $g(\xi)<M$ outside the top-site flat set.
restriction.reason: The released flat-segment proof works with the shape of the zero-one top-site model and expected positions reached by its open paths. Its statements do not identify these quantities with the critical percolation probability. No reason for omitting those further identifications is recorded in the inspected modules.
restriction.impact: The full Theorem 2.1 is certified. Its proof separates directions by $g_{\rm top}(\xi)=1$ or $g_{\rm top}(\xi)<1$; it does not need the missing classification or reverse implication.

results.label: Lemma 2.3
results.title: Two linear bounds for the shape
results.summary: The left and right derivatives of the concave shape give two linear upper bounds for $g$. Both touch $g$ at the chosen interior direction, and each approximates $g$ to first order from its own side.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: Both supporting bounds, their contact with the shape, and their one-sided first-order approximation are certified. This deterministic result uses continuity, homogeneity and concavity of the shape.

results.label: Lemma 3.1
results.title: High-weight paths near a prescribed segment
results.summary: Between any deterministic endpoints separated on scale $s$ and staying away from the coordinate directions, a path has weight close to $g$ of its displacement and stays close to their straight segment, with probability tending to one. The probability estimate is uniform over the permitted endpoint pairs.
definitions: The scale $s$ tends to infinity. Both the permitted loss in weight and the permitted distance from the segment are fixed positive multiples of $s$.

coverage.scope: The certificate covers signed, unbounded weights under the paper's assumptions, with one success-probability bound uniform over all permitted deterministic endpoint pairs.

results.label: Lemma 3.2
results.title: High-weight paths for all endpoint pairs
results.summary: With probability tending to one, every point in one specified level interval can be joined to every point in a later interval. All joining paths stay close to their straight segments and collect nearly the shape-predicted weight, on the same event.
definitions: A level interval consists of the lattice points on $z_1+z_2=I$ between two specified endpoints, for an integer $I$.

coverage.scope: The complete statement for all endpoint pairs on the same event is certified, including unbounded weights. Lemma B.2 supplies the paper's proof under the general weight assumptions.

results.label: Proposition 3.4
results.title: Paths rarely exceed either linear bound
results.summary: In a strip whose length grows much faster than its width, the probability that any directed path exceeds a supporting linear bound by a fixed multiple of the width tends to zero. Either of the two one-sided supporting functions can be used.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The estimate is certified for either supporting linear function and every fixed strip-width factor. The probability bound is uniform once the width and the length-to-width ratio are sufficiently large.

results.label: Lemma 4.1
results.title: Raising finitely many weights at small probability cost
results.summary: A small independent chance to replace each weight by the maximum of itself and a fresh sample raises weights at a controlled probability cost. Outside a small exceptional set of starting values, each selected weight has a uniformly positive chance of a definite increase.

coverage.scope: The linked certificates cover the probability cost of modifying the field, the set of weights that can be increased, and the conditional probability and independence of the increases.

links.label: Good set and conditional independent boosts

results.label: Lemma 4.2
results.title: Crossings of length ⌈s³⌉ become unlikely
results.summary: Outside the directions supported entirely by sites of largest weight, a strip of width proportional to $s$ and length $\lceil s^3\rceil$ becomes unlikely to contain a crossing whose weight is within a fixed multiple of $s$ of the shape prediction.
definitions: The scale $s$ tends to infinity. A crossing joins the two end levels of the strip and stays inside it; its starting point may vary within the first level.

coverage.scope: The complete crossing estimate is certified outside the top-weight flat set, with the paper's strip width, cubic length and weight allowance. A crossing may start anywhere on the strip's first level.

results.label: Proposition 4.3
results.title: The length where crossing probability becomes small
results.summary: A crossing with nearly the shape-predicted weight is likely at lengths comparable to the strip width. The first power-of-two length where its probability drops below a fixed threshold grows faster than the width and is bounded above by the cube of the width.

coverage.scope: The short-length probability limit and all the threshold-length bounds are certified. The certificate uses the first power-of-two threshold length specified in the paper.

results.label: Lemma 4.4
results.title: Infinitely many scales with comparable earlier lengths
results.summary: Infinitely many strip widths have crossing lengths that remain comparable to those at earlier widths. This selects scales where connections built at several smaller widths can be combined without their available lengths decreasing too quickly.

coverage.scope: The complete earlier-scale comparison is certified for the threshold lengths defined by the actual crossing probabilities. It is included in the certificate for Proposition 4.3.

results.label: Lemma 5.7
results.title: Paths between prescribed grid points
results.summary: One event supplies many connecting paths at once. For bounded weights, their endpoints are prescribed lattice approximations to points on parallel lines. For unbounded weights, the paper replaces these endpoints by vertices of paths chosen to avoid very negative weights. Both forms have the bounds needed for Proposition 5.9.

coverage.scope: Both source formulations are certified. Bounded weights allow all prescribed real-center connections. Unbounded weights use the changed endpoints and connection intervals specified in Remark 5.8, which avoid very negative sites.

results.label: Proposition 5.9
results.title: An upper weight bound for every path in a rectangle
results.summary: With probability tending to one, every directed path in a prescribed large rectangle has weight at most a supporting linear value plus a small multiple of the rectangle's width. Both endpoints may be chosen after the weights are observed. The result holds under the full moment assumptions.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The full all-path estimate is certified under the paper's moment assumptions, for every lattice translate of the prescribed rectangle. The released proof supplies the required crossing lengths and simultaneous connections.

results.label: Lemma 6.1
results.title: Probability bound for disjoint path events
results.summary: For any finite list of high-weight path events, requiring the paths to collect disjoint sets of vertices has probability at most the product of the separate probabilities. The weights may have any real-valued distribution; the terminal vertex of each path is excluded from its collected set.

coverage.scope: The full probability inequality for every finite list of these path events is certified, including arbitrary real weight laws and the convention that the terminal vertex is not collected.

results.label: Lemma 6.3
results.title: Paths containing no rare subpath
results.summary: A full stage containing none of the counted high-weight subpaths cannot exceed either supporting linear bound by much. If it ends because it reaches the length threshold before the width threshold, its weight lies strictly below the average of the two supporting values.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.
Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

The counted subpaths either exceed one of the two supporting linear bounds by $\eta s_*$, or cross a specified strip of length $n_*$ and half-width $8s_*$ with weight greater than $n_*g(\xi)-Ks_*$. Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: Both supporting-function bounds are certified, including the stronger loss when a stage reaches its length threshold before its width threshold.

results.label: Lemma 6.5
results.title: Weight bound from a count of rare subpaths
results.summary: For bounded weights, a stage's weight is bounded using the number of disjoint subpaths that exceed a supporting bound or make a nearly shape-weight crossing. A large excess in the stage's weight therefore requires many such subpaths.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.
Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

The counted subpaths either exceed one of the two supporting linear bounds by $\eta s_*$, or cross a specified strip of length $n_*$ and half-width $8s_*$ with weight greater than $n_*g(\xi)-Ks_*$. Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: The complete stage bound is certified. The certificate counts explicit finite collections of disjoint qualifying subpaths; taking their largest possible size gives the paper's formulation.

results.label: Proposition 6.7
results.title: Long paths contain few rare subpaths
results.summary: At a suitably chosen fixed scale, almost surely every sufficiently long path from the origin has fewer than $\lfloor N/32\rfloor$ counted subpaths with disjoint collected vertices, where $N$ is the number of its full stages. The assertion holds simultaneously for all such paths.
definitions: Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

The counted subpaths either exceed one of the two supporting linear bounds by $\eta s_*$, or cross a specified strip of length $n_*$ and half-width $8s_*$ with weight greater than $n_*g(\xi)-Ks_*$. Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: The complete simultaneous bound for every path is certified, including the paper's integer rounding. Counting finite collections of disjoint qualifying subpaths gives the same maximum as the source definition.

results.label: Lemma 6.8
results.title: Path-weight bounds when the shape has a corner
results.summary: If the two one-sided slopes of $g$ differ, each full stage contributes a positive loss relative to the average supporting function. The number of counted high-weight subpaths controls the possible offsets. Summing this estimate gives the bounded-weight contradiction that rules out a corner of $g$.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.
Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: The full-stage and whole-path inequalities are certified for bounded weights. Their unbounded-weight versions, including the correction for large individual weights, are covered by Lemma B.8.

results.label: Lemma A.1
results.title: An infinite up-right path through likely events
results.summary: Events indexed by lattice sites admit an infinite up-right path through successful sites with positive probability, provided failures are uniformly sufficiently unlikely and events at well-separated sites are independent. The path starts at the origin, whose event must also succeed.

coverage.scope: The full statement is certified on any probability space for event families with the required small failure probability and independence at separated sites. The path starts at the origin, whose event is included.

results.label: Lemma B.1
results.title: A lower bound for selected path weights
results.summary: Choose finitely many paths using only the information of which sites satisfy $\omega_z<-T$, and require them to avoid collecting those sites. The lemma bounds the probability that any chosen path has a very negative weight. This permits path selection to depend on the locations of unusually negative weights.
definitions: The threshold $T>0$ is fixed. Path selection may use all indicators $\mathbf1\{\omega_z<-T\}$ but no further weight values. Collected vertices exclude the terminal vertex.
The region $F$ is fixed before observing the weights; it must contain the collected vertices for every possible outcome, rather than only the paths observed in one outcome.
Here $N$ and $n$ are fixed nonnegative integers bounding the number of selected paths and their lengths.
results.notes: The source states its standing shape assumptions by citing Theorem 5.1 and Remark 5.1(ii) of Limiting shape for directed percolation models. The common notation page keeps directional limits separate from the proved uniform approximation.

coverage.scope: The same probability bound is certified when one fixed finite set $F\subset\mathbb Z^2$ contains every collected vertex of every possible selected path. The path selection may still inspect the entire set of sites with weight below $-T$. The matched certificate does not cover random path locations with unbounded range and no common finite containing region. Removing that condition would require an additional argument, for example an exhaustion by finite regions; no such extension was found among uses of this certificate.

links.label: Bound for paths chosen from low-weight sites

restriction.label: Paths confined to a fixed finite region
restriction.paper_scope: The selected family contains at most $N$ paths of length at most $n$. It may depend on all indicators of sites with weight below $-T$, and the possible locations of its paths need not fit in one deterministic finite region.
restriction.certified_scope: The same probability bound is certified when one fixed finite set $F\subset\mathbb Z^2$ contains every collected vertex of every possible selected path. The path selection may still inspect the entire set of sites with weight below $-T$.
restriction.gap: The matched certificate does not cover random path locations with unbounded range and no common finite containing region. Removing that condition would require an additional argument, for example an exhaustion by finite regions; no such extension was found among uses of this certificate.
restriction.reason: The proof splits the product environment into the finitely many coordinates in $F$ and all remaining coordinates, applies the finite-coordinate bound with the outside fixed, then integrates over the outside. This proof is formalized for a fixed finite $F$. That is a boundary of the certificate, not a necessity asserted by the paper.
restriction.impact: The attachment and connection constructions used in the released main proof each lie in a deterministic finite region. This restriction therefore does not alter the hypotheses or conclusion of Theorem 2.1.

results.label: Lemma B.2
results.title: Paths joining every pair of endpoints
results.summary: The simultaneous connection estimate of Lemma 3.2 remains valid for unbounded signed weights under the stated moments. On one event of probability tending to one, all permitted endpoint pairs have paths that remain near their straight segments and collect nearly the shape-predicted weight.
results.notes: Lemma B.2 supplies the general-weight proof of the statement already called Lemma 3.2. It is not an additional hypothesis of Lemma 3.2.

coverage.scope: The full simultaneous connection statement is certified for unbounded weights. One success-probability bound works for every permitted deterministic pair of level intervals.

results.label: Lemma B.3
results.title: Short paths reaching prescribed points
results.summary: Every point of a level interval can be joined by a short path to one of a suitably spaced finite set of points on a later level, with high probability. All these paths have a small lower bound on their weight. A corresponding construction works in the reverse direction.
definitions: A source level interval is a finite interval of lattice points with $\ell(z)=I$, where $I\in\mathbb Z$. A target set consists of deterministic lattice points on level $I+m$, where the integer $m\ge1$ is the required path length. “Prescribed” means chosen before observing the weights.
results.notes: The distinction between choosing a suitable set of endpoints and working with every prescribed suitable set is a restriction in the released statement, not a missing definition.

coverage.scope: For each source interval the release constructs one target set $\mathcal N$ with those geometric conditions, then certifies the forward and backward connections to that set with the paper's path-weight bound. The difference is between “for every admissible $\mathcal N$” and “there exists an admissible $\mathcal N$.” A supplied target set cannot be substituted into the existential certificate. The restriction concerns that choice, not the moment assumptions or the path-weight bound.

links.label: Forward paths to the constructed target set
Backward paths to the constructed target set

restriction.label: One constructed target set
restriction.paper_scope: For each source level interval $\mathcal J$, the path bounds apply to every prescribed deterministic target set $\mathcal N$ satisfying the paper's spacing and endpoint conditions on the later level. The backward statement has the same universal choice of target set.
restriction.certified_scope: For each source interval the release constructs one target set $\mathcal N$ with those geometric conditions, then certifies the forward and backward connections to that set with the paper's path-weight bound.
restriction.gap: The difference is between “for every admissible $\mathcal N$” and “there exists an admissible $\mathcal N$.” A supplied target set cannot be substituted into the existential certificate. The restriction concerns that choice, not the moment assumptions or the path-weight bound.
restriction.reason: The formal proof combines the construction of a common spaced set of target points with the connection estimate. Its input specifies the source interval, not a preselected target set. The inspected files do not record a reason for not exporting the universal target-set version.
restriction.impact: The constructed target sets suffice in the released proof of Lemma B.2 and the later endpoint estimates. The full Theorem 2.1 retains its stated hypotheses and conclusion.

results.label: Lemma B.5
results.title: Paths can go around the very negative vertices
results.summary: With probability tending to one, the obstructions created by very negative weights occur in bounded groups. Paths can then follow a prescribed direction while avoiding those weights, with uniformly bounded displacement from the line. The same construction supplies the endpoint adjustments needed to join these paths to crossings.

coverage.scope: The probability estimate and all five geometric conclusions are certified in separate declarations. These include forward and backward avoidance, bounded displacement from a line, joining paths, path intersections and endpoint adjustments, using the neighborhoods specified in the selected draft.

results.label: Lemma B.6
results.title: A lower weight bound for many chosen paths
results.summary: A family of short paths may be chosen after observing the locations of very negative weights. If it avoids those sites, the probability that any member has an excessively negative weight tends to zero, even when the number of candidate paths grows polynomially with the scale.

coverage.scope: The bound is certified for every permitted finite path family selected from the indicators of very negative weights. The certificate preserves the paper's size and length limits and its relation between the counting exponent and the negative moment order.

results.label: Lemma B.7
results.title: Large positive weights do not spoil the connections
results.summary: The positive moment assumption controls very large weights throughout the regions used for connections. Requiring each trial rectangle to contain no such weight still leaves a fixed positive crossing probability, and the crossing events in disjoint rectangles remain independent.

coverage.scope: The bounds for the large region and the smaller rectangles, and the probability and independence of the modified crossing trials, are all certified. They appear in separate declarations.

links.label: No heavy vertex in working region

results.label: Lemma B.8
results.title: The path bounds with unbounded weights
results.summary: The stage and whole-path estimates remain valid for weights without a uniform upper bound after adding an explicit correction for the weight collected above a chosen threshold. This separates the contribution of individual large weights from the number of counted high-weight subpaths.
definitions: Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

The counted subpaths either exceed one of the two supporting linear bounds by $\eta s_*$, or cross a specified strip of length $n_*$ and half-width $8s_*$ with weight greater than $n_*g(\xi)-Ks_*$. Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.
For a fixed threshold $M_0$, the correction on a path $\pi$ is $\sum_{z\text{ collected by }\pi}(\omega_z-M_0)^+$, where $a^+=\max\{a,0\}$.

coverage.scope: The stage, full-stage and whole-path bounds are certified. The correction uses exactly the amount above the weight cutoff, summed over the blocks actually visited by the path.

links.label: Excess bounded by itinerary block sum

results.label: Lemma B.9
results.title: Bounding the contribution of large positive weights
results.summary: Almost surely, the total amount by which weights exceed a chosen threshold is eventually small on every sufficiently long connected collection of relevant blocks. This holds simultaneously for all such collections and therefore controls the correction for every long path.
definitions: A block is one of the overlapping rectangles used to contain a stage. Connected collections are joined by neighboring block indices; they need not be fixed before the weights are observed.

coverage.scope: The uniform bound over connected block collections and its application to every path are certified. The certificate preserves the source's parameter dependence, with its constant chosen before the direction and scale.

results.label: Remark 3.3
results.title: Choosing short paths after observing low weights
results.summary: For bounded weights, the short connections between level intervals may be deterministic. The general-weight version allows them to depend on the locations of very negative sites.
definitions: A level interval consists of the lattice points on $z_1+z_2=I$ between two specified endpoints, for an integer $I$.

coverage.scope: No separate certificate is assigned to this explanation. The mathematical path-connection conclusions are covered by Lemmas 3.2 and B.2.

results.label: Remark 3.5
results.title: The same bound for strips with any center
results.summary: The strip estimate of Proposition 3.4 extends to any integer starting level and any real center. Enlarging the half-width from $Rs$ to $(R+1)s$ absorbs the rounding used to place the strip inside a lattice translate of an origin-centered strip.
definitions: Here $s\ge1$ is the width scale and $R>0$ is fixed. The strip's center is measured in the coordinate $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$ for a fixed interior direction $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$.

coverage.scope: Exact translation for lattice-centered strips and the rounded instances used in Proposition 5.9 are certified. This review has not completed the correspondence for the remark's full arbitrary-real-center quantifier; a missing standalone theorem name does not establish a mathematical restriction.

links.label: Endpoint argument using translated strip bounds

results.label: Remark 5.1
results.title: Which connections require changes for unbounded weights
results.summary: The all-endpoint estimate of Proposition 5.9 holds under the main moment assumptions, including signed unbounded weights. The bounded- and general-weight formulations use different short connections.

coverage.scope: This is an explanation of the proof, rather than a separate theorem. The corresponding mathematical statements are recorded at Lemma 5.7, Remark 5.8 and Proposition 5.9.

results.label: Remark 5.2
results.title: The connecting paths are shorter than the proof needs
results.summary: The deterministic connecting paths have at most $16C_*s_k$ steps. The proof retains the weaker bound $8C_*k^2s_k$ because it already yields the needed probability estimates; the sharper length observation is not needed for the differentiability conclusion.
definitions: Here $s_k=2^k$, and $C_*=50/\min\{\xi_1,1-\xi_1\}$ for the fixed interior direction $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$.

coverage.scope: The weaker connecting-path length bound used in the paper's probability estimates is certified. The sharper arithmetic is proved separately, but its combination for every path in the source family has not been fully checked. The weaker bound suffices for Theorem 2.1.

links.label: Staircase lower-tail bound with the retained length budget

results.label: Remark 5.3
results.title: Choose the connecting paths after locating negative weights
results.summary: The general-weight connection statement allows paths chosen from the locations of very negative sites. All selected paths avoid collecting those sites and satisfy a simultaneous lower weight bound.

coverage.scope: The simultaneous lower weight estimate is certified for paths selected from the low-weight indicators. Separate certificates construct the paths and show that their collected vertices avoid all sites below the chosen negative threshold.

results.label: Remark 5.4
results.title: The weight error on a short connecting interval
results.summary: On short grid intervals, the connection follows a path chosen to avoid very negative sites. Its lower weight estimate controls the difference between its weight and either supporting linear value.
definitions: The error scale is $t_k=\varepsilon_0 2^k/k$, where $k\ge1$ is an integer and $\varepsilon_0>0$ is fixed. A supporting linear function is a linear upper bound for $g$ that agrees with $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The short-interval estimate with additive error $t_k/2$ follows from the certified path-weight lower bound and transverse-location bound. The final exported grid theorem states the weaker common allowance $2t_k$. This changes the presentation of the local estimate, not the paper's mathematical coverage.

links.label: Half-error input and local cost arithmetic

results.label: Remark 5.5
results.title: Independent crossings with no very large weight
results.summary: The longer-interval construction uses independent crossings in disjoint rectangles. Requiring the weights in each rectangle to remain below the chosen threshold reduces the success probability by at most half. The probability that every trial fails therefore decreases exponentially in the number of trials.

coverage.scope: The reduced success probability, independence across disjoint rectangles and exponential bound on failure of every trial are certified for the modified crossing events.

results.label: Remark 5.6
results.title: The weight error when a crossing needs two connections
results.summary: On long grid intervals, a successful crossing is shortened by a bounded number of vertices and joined at both ends to paths avoiding very negative weights. The resulting connection stays in the required strip and has a controlled loss relative to either supporting linear value.
definitions: The error scale is $t_k=\varepsilon_0 2^k/k$, where $k\ge1$ is an integer and $\varepsilon_0>0$ is fixed. A supporting linear function is a linear upper bound for $g$ that agrees with $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The long-interval estimate with additive error $3t_k/2$ follows by joining the certified arrival path, trimmed crossing and final connection. The final exported grid theorem permits the weaker common allowance $2t_k$. The modified crossing probability and location bound are also certified.

links.label: Merge and tail with combined error allowance
Assembly of the local cost bound

results.label: Remark 5.8
results.title: The grid statement with random endpoints
results.summary: For unbounded weights, the grid connections end on paths selected to avoid very negative sites. The source claims this only for the grid intervals used to reach or leave an endpoint in Proposition 5.9. That modified statement, rather than every prescribed line position, is certified.

coverage.scope: The source's modified statement is certified with its selected random endpoints and the specified intervals for reaching or leaving an endpoint. The all-real-center clause of Lemma 5.7 belongs to its bounded-weight formulation.

results.label: Remark 5.10
results.title: Removing a few endpoint vertices preserves the path bound
results.summary: The general-weight all-endpoint estimate retains the conclusion of Proposition 5.9. It permits endpoint adjustments of a bounded number of steps, with negligible discarded weight at the required scale.

coverage.scope: The full general-weight conclusion of Proposition 5.9 is certified, together with the endpoint shortening and lower- and upper-connection construction used here.

results.label: Remark 6.2
results.title: Choosing a scale for unbounded weights
results.summary: Discusses the parameter choice for unbounded weights, including a scale-dependent upper cutoff and the correction for weights above it. This is a parameter discussion rather than a separate theorem.

coverage.scope: This is an explanation of how the proof chooses its parameters, rather than a separately stated theorem. Its correspondence with a separate certificate has not been assessed.

results.label: Remark 6.4
results.title: The cost of moving across a corner
results.summary: When the left and right slopes of $g$ differ, moving sideways contributes a positive loss relative to their average supporting function. The loss is proportional to the slope difference and to the sideways displacement. This is the quantitative step that makes a corner incompatible with long near-optimal paths.
definitions: A supporting linear function is a linear function that is at least $g$ everywhere in $\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2$ and equals $g$ at the direction under consideration.

coverage.scope: The quantitative loss caused by reaching the sideways displacement threshold is certified. The discussion of why that loss vanishes when the two slopes agree is explanatory.

results.label: Remark 6.6
results.title: Subtracting the weight above a threshold
results.summary: The general-weight stage estimate contains an explicit correction for weights above a fixed cutoff. It extends the bounded-weight inequality to weights without a uniform upper bound.
definitions: Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

coverage.scope: The one-step and stage inequalities are certified, subtracting exactly the amount above the chosen cutoff at the collected vertices.

results.label: Remark 6.9
results.title: The large-weight correction stays small
results.summary: The positive moment estimate makes the accumulated contribution above the cutoff smaller than the loss forced by a putative corner. After combining this with the bound on counted high-weight subpaths, every long path still loses a positive amount per stage, contradicting the shape limit.
definitions: Fix $\xi=(\xi_1,1-\xi_1)$ with $0<\xi_1<1$. Put $r(z)=z_1-\xi_1(z_1+z_2)$; this measures displacement from the line in direction $\xi$.

A stage ends when a path first reaches $2n_*$ steps or changes its $r$ coordinate by at least $s_*$. Here $n_*,s_*>0$ are fixed length and width scales. A stage ending at one of these thresholds is full; the final shorter piece is a remainder.

The counted subpaths either exceed one of the two supporting linear bounds by $\eta s_*$, or cross a specified strip of length $n_*$ and half-width $8s_*$ with weight greater than $n_*g(\xi)-Ks_*$. Here $\eta,K>0$ are fixed constants. Disjointness concerns collected vertices, so a terminal vertex may be shared.

coverage.scope: The whole-path estimate, the eventual bound on weights above the cutoff and the resulting positive loss are certified. The claim that this is the proof's only use of a positive moment above order four has not been audited.

results.label: Remark B.4
results.title: Why this proof needs a moment above one
results.summary: Discusses a proposed logarithmic-moment alternative to the negative moment of order greater than one. Neither the paper nor this guide claims that the theorem has been proved under that proposed assumption.
results.notes: Do not label the suggested logarithmic-moment condition as a proved theorem or as an assumption needed by the certified main theorem.

coverage.scope: This is an explanation of the proof and a proposed weakening of its assumptions. No certificate for the proposed logarithmic-moment result is identified here.

results.label: Remark B.10
results.title: Why this proof requires a positive moment above four
results.summary: Discusses the positive moment of order greater than four and a conditional improvement under a better crossing-length estimate. That improvement is not asserted as a proved result.

coverage.scope: The proposed conditional improvement and the necessary tail condition discussed in this remark have not been matched to certificates. The release proves the theorem with a positive moment of order greater than four.

results.label: Appendix C.1
results.title: A law with no finite uniform shape limit
results.summary: For every $0<p<1$, the example gives a weight law with finite negative moment of order $p$ but no finite uniform shape limit. Along infinitely many interior endpoints, the last-passage time divided by endpoint distance becomes arbitrarily negative.
definitions: The endpoints lie in a fixed cone bounded away from the coordinate axes. The uniform limit concerns all sufficiently distant lattice endpoints in that cone at once.

coverage.scope: For every moment order strictly between zero and one, the law's construction, its moment properties and the almost-sure failure of a finite uniform shape limit along the specified interior endpoints are certified.
